title: Start with the Business Conversation
moduleName: Turn a Speaking Engagement into New Business
learningGoal: Identify what happens after somebody has heard you speak and define one natural next action that turns audience attention into a follow-up opportunity.

items.title: Applause Is Not a Business Model
items.description: A room full of applause is valuable, but it does not provide a way to follow up. Without a system, even the best talk becomes a one-time event with no lasting business impact.

items.title: One Natural Next Action
items.description: Every talk needs one clear next step. Not five options — one simple, relevant action that moves an interested attendee toward a conversation.

items.title: The Chain
items.description: Talk → useful gift → form submission → email delivery → optional appointment. Each link depends on the one before it.

items.title: Audience
items.description: Who is in the room? Be specific about their role, industry, and the problem they share.

items.title: Pressing Issue
items.description: What problem did your talk address? The resource and follow-up must connect directly to this same issue.

items.title: Next Conversation
items.description: What 15- or 20-minute call would be genuinely useful to someone who found your talk valuable?

items.title: Speaker
items.description: Leadership Reset Checklist after a leadership keynote; invite attendees to a workplace leadership discussion.

items.title: Coach
items.description: 7 Questions to Find Your Next Goal after a coaching workshop; invite to an introductory session.

items.title: Consultant
items.description: Process Waste Scorecard after a business systems talk; invite to a discovery call.

items.title: Trainer
items.description: Team Training Needs Checklist after a learning session; invite to a needs review.

items.title: Service Business
items.description: Maintenance Risk Checklist after a customer education presentation; invite to an assessment.

keyPoint: A talk without a follow-up system is a missed opportunity. Define one natural next action before you design anything else. The resource, form, and follow-up must all serve the same audience and the same problem your talk addressed.

actionSteps.title: Choose Your Talk
actionSteps.description: Write your talk title and the audience in your workbook.

actionSteps.title: Define the Problem
actionSteps.description: Identify the pressing issue your talk addresses and the one 15- or 20-minute call worth offering.

actionSteps.title: Complete Workbook Page 2
actionSteps.description: Map the talk title, audience, problem, and next conversation. Verify they all connect to the same theme.

quizzes.question: What is the main problem with relying on applause alone after a talk?

options.option_text: Applause makes the speaker overconfident
Applause does not provide a way to follow up with interested attendees
Applause is too loud and distracting
Audiences rarely applaud anymore

quizzes.explanation: Applause feels good but creates no business outcome. Without a follow-up system, even the best talk becomes a one-time event with no lasting impact.

quizzes.question: How many natural next actions should each talk have?

options.option_text: None — let the audience decide what to do
As many as possible to increase chances
At least three options for flexibility
One clear, relevant next action

quizzes.explanation: Every talk needs one clear next step. Multiple options create decision paralysis. One simple, relevant action moves interested attendees toward a conversation.

quizzes.question: What must the resource and follow-up offer connect to?

options.option_text: The speaker's most expensive service
The same audience problem the talk addressed
The event organizer's priorities
A different topic to show range

quizzes.explanation: The resource and follow-up must connect directly to the problem your talk addressed. Relevance makes the gift useful and creates a natural next conversation.

title: Create the Free Resource
moduleName: Turn a Speaking Engagement into New Business
learningGoal: Produce a small, relevant lead magnet that the audience can use within 10 minutes and that creates a natural next conversation.

items.title: Quick to Use
items.description: The audience should be able to use the gift within 10 minutes. If it requires hours of work, it will sit in their downloads folder unused.

items.title: Practical Formats
items.description: Good choices: checklist, scorecard, worksheet, cheat sheet, template, mini-guide, or diagnostic. These are immediately actionable.

items.title: Not a Brochure
items.description: Avoid making the resource a product brochure. The goal is genuine usefulness, not a disguised sales pitch.

items.title: Title
items.description: Clear and specific. Example: 5-Minute Leadership Reset Checklist.

items.title: One-Sentence Promise
items.description: What will they be able to do after using it? Example: Identify the three habits most damaging your team's focus.

items.title: 3-5 Steps
items.description: Enough to be useful, not so many that it overwhelms. Each step should be actionable.

items.title: Useful Example
items.description: Show what good looks like. One completed example helps people start immediately.

items.title: Next Action
items.description: What should they do after completing the resource? This bridges naturally to your follow-up offer.

items.title: Export as PDF
items.description: PDF is the most reliable format for sharing. It looks professional and works on any device.

items.title: Stable Download Location
items.description: Store the PDF at a URL that will not change. Use your website, a file hosting service, or a document management system.

items.title: Test the Download
items.description: Download the file yourself on both desktop and mobile. Verify it opens correctly and looks as intended.

keyPoint: The best lead magnets are not the most comprehensive — they are the most immediately useful. A one-page checklist that someone uses today is worth more than a 50-page guide they never open. Build for action, not for impressiveness.

actionSteps.title: Choose Your Format
actionSteps.description: Select checklist, scorecard, worksheet, cheat sheet, template, or mini-guide based on your talk content.

actionSteps.title: Draft the Resource
actionSteps.description: Write title, promise, 3-5 steps, one example, and next action. Keep it to one page if possible.

actionSteps.title: Export and Test
actionSteps.description: Export as PDF, upload to a stable location, and test the download on desktop and mobile. Record the URL in your workbook.

quizzes.question: How long should it take the audience to use the free resource?

options.option_text: A full day of focused work
Several hours to get full value
Within 10 minutes
It depends on the complexity of the topic

quizzes.explanation: The audience should be able to use the gift within 10 minutes. If it requires hours of work, it will sit unused. Quick wins create positive associations with your brand.

quizzes.question: Which of these is NOT a good format for a speaking-event lead magnet?

options.option_text: A product brochure disguised as a guide
A one-page checklist
A simple scorecard
A worksheet with 5 prompts

quizzes.explanation: Avoid making the resource a product brochure. The goal is genuine usefulness, not a disguised sales pitch. Brochures feel promotional and reduce trust.

quizzes.question: What should you include at the end of the resource?

options.option_text: A lengthy biography of the speaker
A request to share on social media
A detailed price list of all services
A clear next action that bridges to your follow-up offer

quizzes.explanation: The resource should end with a clear next action. This bridges naturally to your follow-up offer and makes the path from resource to conversation obvious.

title: Build the Capture Form
moduleName: Turn a Speaking Engagement into New Business
learningGoal: Create a simple form that collects only necessary details, explains the purpose of collection, and includes appropriate privacy and consent handling.

items.title: Minimal Fields
items.description: Only collect what you need. First Name and Email are usually enough. Every extra field reduces completion rates.

items.title: Privacy Notice
items.description: Explain why you are collecting details and how you will use them. Link to your privacy policy. This builds trust and may be legally required.

items.title: Separate Consent
items.description: When follow-up requires marketing consent, make it a separate optional choice. Do not make SMS consent compulsory in return for a resource.

items.title: Menu Path
items.description: Sites → Forms → + Create New Form

items.title: Form Name
items.description: Use a clear naming convention: M22 | [Event] | Resource Request. This makes submissions easy to find later.

items.title: Required Fields
items.description: First Name and Email as required. Consider one optional dropdown asking their biggest challenge for segmentation.

items.title: Test Submission
items.description: Submit using your own test email. Confirm it appears in Sites → Forms → Submissions and in Contacts.

items.title: Too Many Fields
items.description: Phone, company, job title, budget — each extra field reduces completions. Only ask for what you truly need.

items.title: Compulsory Marketing Consent
items.description: Do not require marketing consent to receive the resource. The resource is the exchange for contact details; marketing consent is separate.

items.title: Unclear Purpose
items.description: Vague forms feel suspicious. Clearly state what they will receive and what happens next.

keyPoint: A form is a transaction, not a survey. Every field you add reduces completions. Collect only what you need, be transparent about why, and keep marketing consent separate. A simple form with high completion beats a detailed form with low submission.

actionSteps.title: Create the Form
actionSteps.description: Navigate to Sites → Forms and create a new form with First Name and Email as required fields.

actionSteps.title: Add Privacy Text
actionSteps.description: Include a brief explanation of how you will use their details and link to your privacy notice.

actionSteps.title: Test and Verify
actionSteps.description: Submit using your own test email. Confirm the submission appears in both Forms → Submissions and Contacts.

nextLessonTitle: Create the Funnel and Thank-You Page

quizzes.question: Which two fields are usually enough for a simple resource request form?

options.option_text: First Name, Last Name, Email, Phone, Company
First Name and Email
Email only — names are not needed
Full address and postal code

quizzes.explanation: First Name and Email are usually enough. Every extra field reduces completion rates. Only collect what you truly need for follow-up.

quizzes.question: Should marketing consent be required to receive the free resource?

options.option_text: Yes, consent is required for all form submissions
It depends on the event size
No, marketing consent should be a separate optional choice
Only if the resource is valuable

quizzes.explanation: Do not make marketing consent compulsory in return for a resource. The resource is the exchange for contact details; marketing consent is a separate optional choice.

quizzes.question: Where should you check that test submissions appear?

options.option_text: In the Analytics dashboard only
Both Forms → Submissions and Contacts
Only in the Forms section
Only in your email inbox

quizzes.explanation: Test submissions should appear in both Forms → Submissions and Contacts. This confirms the form is connected properly and creates a contact record for workflow triggers.

title: Create the Funnel and Thank-You Page
moduleName: Turn a Speaking Engagement into New Business
learningGoal: Build a mobile-friendly landing page and thank-you experience that makes requesting the resource simple and sets up the next action.

items.title: Capture Page
items.description: Benefit headline, description of the free gift, short form, reassuring privacy line, and a clear button: Send me the checklist.

items.title: Thank-You Page
items.description: Confirm the request is on its way, provide a direct resource link if appropriate, and offer a separate optional booking button.

items.title: Mobile First
items.description: Most QR scans happen on phones. Test every element on mobile before publishing.

items.title: Menu Path
items.description: Sites → Funnels

items.title: Funnel Name
items.description: Use a clear name: M22 | [Event] | Speaker Gift. This keeps your funnels organized.

items.title: Public URL
items.description: Publish and copy the public landing-page URL. Do not point the QR at an editor or preview URL.

items.title: HTTPS Test
items.description: The public page must load over HTTPS. Test it outside the editor on both desktop and mobile.

items.title: Headline
items.description: Lead with the benefit, not the speaker name. Example: Get the 5-Minute Leadership Reset Checklist.

items.title: Description
items.description: Two sentences about what they will receive and why it matters. Keep it brief.

items.title: Form
items.description: Embed the form you built in Lesson 3. Keep it visible without scrolling on mobile.

items.title: Privacy Line
items.description: Reassure them: We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime. Link to your full policy.

keyPoint: The funnel is where interest becomes action. A mobile-friendly page with a clear benefit, simple form, and reassuring privacy line will outperform a beautiful but confusing page every time. Test on your phone before you show it to an audience.

actionSteps.title: Create the Funnel
actionSteps.description: Navigate to Sites → Funnels and create a two-step funnel with capture and thank-you pages.

actionSteps.title: Build the Capture Page
actionSteps.description: Add benefit headline, description, embedded form, privacy line, and clear call-to-action button.

actionSteps.title: Build the Thank-You Page
actionSteps.description: Confirm the request, provide resource link, and offer an optional booking button.

actionSteps.title: Test on Mobile
actionSteps.description: Open the published URL on your phone and submit the form. Verify the experience works smoothly.

quizzes.question: How many steps should the funnel have?

options.option_text: One page with everything on it
Two steps: capture page and thank-you page
It depends on the event size
At least five pages for completeness

quizzes.explanation: A two-step funnel works best: capture page for the form, thank-you page for confirmation and next steps. More steps create friction; one page can feel cluttered.

quizzes.question: What type of URL should you use for the QR code destination?

options.option_text: A private internal link
The editor or preview URL
A link to your main website homepage
The published public URL over HTTPS

quizzes.explanation: Always use the published public URL over HTTPS. Editor or preview URLs will not work for attendees. The public URL is what they will actually scan and visit.

quizzes.question: Why should you test the funnel on a mobile phone?

options.option_text: Only iPhone users scan QR codes
Phones have better screens than projectors
Most QR scans happen on phones, so mobile experience is critical
Mobile testing is optional if desktop looks good

quizzes.explanation: Most QR scans happen on phones. If the mobile experience is poor — form fields too small, buttons hard to tap, page slow to load — attendees will abandon before submitting.

title: Generate a QR Code
moduleName: Turn a Speaking Engagement into New Business
learningGoal: Create a dynamic QR code that points to the published funnel page and is scannable from a projected slide.

items.title: Instant Access
items.description: A QR code removes the friction of typing a URL. One scan opens the page immediately.

items.title: Dynamic Codes
items.description: Native HighLevel QR codes are dynamic. You can change the destination later without generating a new code.

items.title: Not a Lead Capture
items.description: A QR scan opens a URL. It does not collect personal details or establish consent until the visitor submits the form.

items.title: Menu Path
items.description: Sites → QR Codes → Create QR Code

items.title: Name
items.description: Use a clear name: M22 | [Event] | Resource QR. This keeps your QR codes organized.

items.title: Destination
items.description: Choose Funnel or Website as the destination type. Select the published funnel page or paste its URL.

items.title: High Contrast
items.description: Customize with high contrast for better scanning. Dark code on light background works best.

items.title: Multi-Device Test
items.description: Scan with two different phones (or a phone plus a separate device). Verify the link points to the correct page.

items.title: Short URL Fallback
items.description: Keep a visible short URL as a fallback for anyone who cannot or prefers not to scan.

items.title: Projector Test
items.description: Test the QR at projected-slide size, not just close to the screen. It must work from the back of the room.

keyPoint: A QR code is a bridge, not a destination. It must be large enough, high contrast enough, and point to a live URL that works on mobile. Test from the back of the room, not just from your desk. A broken QR code wastes the entire talk.

actionSteps.title: Create the QR Code
actionSteps.description: Navigate to Sites → QR Codes and create a new code pointing to your published funnel page.

actionSteps.title: Customize and Download
actionSteps.description: Use high contrast, download PNG or SVG, and save with a clear filename.

actionSteps.title: Test Thoroughly
actionSteps.description: Scan with multiple devices, verify the destination, and test from a distance similar to the back of a room.

nextLessonTitle: Make the QR Slide and Spoken Invitation

quizzes.question: What does a QR code do on its own?

options.option_text: It sends an email to the scanner automatically
It opens a destination URL; it does not collect data or establish consent
It automatically collects contact details from anyone who scans it
It books an appointment in the speaker's calendar

quizzes.explanation: A QR code only opens a URL. It does not collect personal details or establish consent until the visitor submits a form. Do not confuse scans with leads.

quizzes.question: Why are dynamic QR codes better than static ones?

options.option_text: They are required by law
They look more professional
They scan faster
You can change the destination later without generating a new code

quizzes.explanation: Dynamic QR codes let you change the destination URL later. If you update your funnel or run the same talk at multiple events, you can adjust the destination without redesigning your slide.

quizzes.question: How should you test the QR code?

options.option_text: Scan it once from your desk
Only test on the newest iPhone
Testing is not necessary for HighLevel QR codes
Test with multiple devices and from a distance like the back of a room

quizzes.explanation: Test with multiple devices and from a realistic distance. A QR that works when held close to the screen may fail when projected at the back of a large room.

title: Make the QR Slide and Spoken Invitation
moduleName: Turn a Speaking Engagement into New Business
learningGoal: Design a presentation slide that presents the QR offer clearly and practice a spoken invitation that feels natural, not salesy.

items.title: Big QR Code
items.description: The QR should be the largest element on the slide. Leave enough quiet space around it for reliable scanning.

items.title: Benefit Headline
items.description: One line stating what they get. Example: Get the 5-Minute Leadership Checklist.

items.title: Short Description
items.description: One sentence about what it does. Keep it visible and readable from the back row.

items.title: Short URL
items.description: Include a visible short URL as a fallback for anyone who cannot scan.

items.title: Natural Timing
items.description: Show the QR slide while discussing the next useful step, and again at Q&A or the end. Do not interrupt your talk to pitch.

items.title: Suggested Script
items.description: We have covered a lot. I have put the key actions into a short worksheet you can use today. Scan this QR code and I will send it to your inbox. If you would like to talk through your situation, there is also an optional booking link afterward.

items.title: Under 20 Seconds
items.description: Practice until you can deliver the invitation in under 20 seconds. Brevity respects the audience's time.

items.title: Too Early
items.description: Do not show the QR in the first five minutes. The audience needs to trust your content before they want your resource.

items.title: Too Pushy
items.description: Avoid language that pressures. Let the QR be an invitation, not a demand.

items.title: Cluttered Slide
items.description: Too much text, too many colors, or competing elements make the QR hard to find and scan.

keyPoint: The QR slide is not an advertisement — it is a service. Present it as a natural next step for people who found your talk valuable. A clear slide plus a brief, practiced invitation will outperform a flashy slide plus an awkward pitch every time.

actionSteps.title: Design the Slide
actionSteps.description: Create a slide with large QR code, benefit headline, short description, and visible short URL.

actionSteps.title: Write Your Script
actionSteps.description: Draft a 15-20 second spoken invitation that feels natural and explains the benefit.

actionSteps.title: Practice Aloud
actionSteps.description: Practice the sentence aloud with the QR visible on screen. Time yourself and refine until it feels natural.

quizzes.question: When should you show the QR slide during your talk?

options.option_text: Continuously throughout the entire presentation
In the first five minutes to capture attention
Only after everyone has applauded
While discussing the next useful step, and again at Q&A or the end

quizzes.explanation: Show the QR while discussing the next useful step, and again at Q&A or the end. The audience needs to trust your content before they want your resource. Too early feels pushy; too late misses engaged attendees.

quizzes.question: How long should the spoken invitation take?

options.option_text: At least two minutes to explain all benefits
It depends on the audience size
As long as needed to cover every feature
Under 20 seconds

quizzes.explanation: Practice until you can deliver the invitation in under 20 seconds. Brevity respects the audience's time and prevents the invitation from feeling like a sales pitch.

quizzes.question: What should be the largest element on the QR slide?

options.option_text: The speaker's logo and branding
The QR code itself
Testimonials from previous attendees
A detailed description of the resource

quizzes.explanation: The QR code should be the largest element. It must be scannable from the back of the room. Branding and descriptions are secondary to the code's visibility and function.

title: Build the Follow-Up Workflow
moduleName: Turn a Speaking Engagement into New Business
learningGoal: Create an automated workflow that delivers the promised resource, tags the lead, and provides appropriate next steps without being pushy.

items.title: Trigger
items.description: Form Submitted, filtered to the specific event form. A QR scan without a form submission does not fire this trigger.

items.title: Tag
items.description: Add Contact Tag: Event | [Event Name] | Resource Requested. This segments leads by event for future reference.

items.title: Immediate Email
items.description: Subject: Here is your [resource name]. Include a working download link. Deliver what you promised, instantly.

items.title: Wait 2 Days
items.description: Give them time to use the resource before following up.

items.title: Email 2
items.description: One related tip plus a simple question. Keep it helpful, not salesy.

items.title: Wait 3 More Days
items.description: Space out messages to avoid overwhelming.

items.title: Email 3
items.description: Offer the booking link to a relevant introductory conversation. Make it optional, not demanding.

items.title: Verify Permissions
items.description: Confirm opt-in permissions before sending marketing messages. Include unsubscribe controls.

items.title: Stop on Reply
items.description: Configure the workflow to stop or branch on reply. A reply indicates engagement that deserves a human response.

items.title: Avoid Duplicates
items.description: Do not send duplicate emails from both Form Autoresponder and Workflow. Choose one delivery method.

items.title: Test Before Publishing
items.description: Test on an internal email. Confirm delivery, contact tag, and later actions. Use shortened test waits, then restore real delays.

keyPoint: The follow-up workflow is where promises are kept. Deliver the resource instantly, tag the lead for segmentation, nurture with helpful content, and invite a conversation only after providing value. A workflow that delivers on its promises builds trust; one that spams destroys it.

actionSteps.title: Create the Workflow
actionSteps.description: Navigate to Automation → Workflows and create a new workflow named M22 | [Event] | Speaker Follow-Up.

actionSteps.title: Add Trigger and Actions
actionSteps.description: Add Form Submitted trigger filtered to your specific form. Add tag, immediate email, waits, and nurture emails.

actionSteps.title: Configure Protections
actionSteps.description: Add stop-on-reply, unsubscribe controls, and verify no duplicate delivery from Form Autoresponder.

actionSteps.title: Test Thoroughly
actionSteps.description: Test on an internal email. Confirm delivery, tag, and later actions. Use shortened test waits if needed.

quizzes.question: What trigger should start the resource delivery workflow?

options.option_text: QR Code Scanned
Appointment Booked
Form Submitted, filtered to the specific event form
Contact Created

quizzes.explanation: Use Form Submitted filtered to the specific event form. A QR scan without a form submission does not fire this trigger. Only form submissions indicate genuine interest.

quizzes.question: Why should you avoid duplicate email delivery from both Form Autoresponder and Workflow?

options.option_text: It costs more to send two emails
HighLevel does not allow both to be active
Receiving the same email twice looks unprofessional and annoys contacts
Duplicate emails are required for deliverability

quizzes.explanation: Duplicate delivery looks unprofessional and annoys contacts. Choose one method: either the Form Autoresponder or the Workflow, not both.

quizzes.question: What should happen when a contact replies to a workflow email?

options.option_text: Continue sending automated messages as planned
Automatically book an appointment for them
Stop or branch the workflow to allow human response
Send them a discount code immediately

quizzes.explanation: A reply indicates engagement that deserves a human response. Configure the workflow to stop or branch on reply so you can respond personally rather than sending more automated messages.

title: Add a Booking Calendar
moduleName: Turn a Speaking Engagement into New Business
learningGoal: Create a simple booking calendar that lets interested people choose a time voluntarily, and integrate it into the thank-you page and follow-up emails.

items.title: Menu Path
items.description: Calendars → Calendar Settings → + New Calendar (or Settings → Calendars in some layouts)

items.title: Duration
items.description: Create a 15- or 20-minute Personal Booking calendar. Short enough to feel low-commitment, long enough to be useful.

items.title: Configuration
items.description: Set host, availability, location or video connection, booking rules, and confirmation settings.

items.title: Share Link
items.description: Use Share to copy the permanent booking link. This is what you will put on the thank-you page and in emails.

items.title: Thank-You Page
items.description: Put the booking link on the thank-you page as a separate optional button. Do not make it the primary action.

items.title: Follow-Up Email
items.description: Include the booking link in Email 3 of the nurture sequence. Present it as an option, not a requirement.

items.title: Test Booking
items.description: Test a time on your phone and then cancel the test appointment. Verify the confirmation email and calendar entry work correctly.

items.title: Voluntary Choice
items.description: The attendee chooses a time. Do not use the workflow Book Appointment action to place attendees into appointments without their choosing.

items.title: Optional Not Required
items.description: Booking is always optional. Some people will want the resource without a call. Respect their choice.

items.title: Working Availability
items.description: Keep your calendar updated. Nothing destroys trust faster than booking a time that the host cannot honor.

keyPoint: A booking calendar is an invitation, not an assignment. Let interested people choose a time that works for them. Make it optional, keep it updated, and present it as a natural next step rather than a requirement. The best bookings come from people who genuinely want to talk, not from those who feel pressured.

actionSteps.title: Create the Calendar
actionSteps.description: Navigate to Calendars and create a 15- or 20-minute booking calendar with your availability.

actionSteps.title: Copy the Share Link
actionSteps.description: Use the Share feature to copy the permanent booking link.

actionSteps.title: Add to Thank-You Page and Email
actionSteps.description: Put the link on the thank-you page and in Email 3 of the nurture sequence.

actionSteps.title: Test and Verify
actionSteps.description: Book a test appointment on your phone, verify confirmation, then cancel. Record the URL in your workbook.

quizzes.question: How long should the booking calendar appointment be?

options.option_text: As short as possible — 5 minutes is ideal
It depends on the speaker's usual rate
15 or 20 minutes
At least one hour to cover everything

quizzes.explanation: A 15- or 20-minute calendar works best. It is short enough to feel low-commitment but long enough to be genuinely useful. Longer durations create resistance; shorter durations feel rushed.

quizzes.question: Should you automatically book appointments for attendees using a workflow action?

options.option_text: Only for attendees who downloaded the resource
Only if they provided phone number
Yes, it saves time and ensures follow-up
No, the attendee must choose a time voluntarily

quizzes.explanation: Never use the workflow Book Appointment action to place attendees into appointments without their choosing. The attendee must select a time voluntarily. Auto-booking without consent is disrespectful and counterproductive.

quizzes.question: Where should you place the booking link?

options.option_text: In every message you send
On the thank-you page and in the nurture sequence email
Only in the first email immediately after form submission
Only on your main website

quizzes.explanation: Place the booking link on the thank-you page as an optional next step, and include it in Email 3 of the nurture sequence. This gives people multiple chances to book without feeling pressured.

title: Rehearse, Launch, and Measure
moduleName: Turn a Speaking Engagement into New Business
learningGoal: Complete a full end-to-end test of the speaker-to-client system and establish metrics to measure whether the talk is producing business opportunities.

items.title: Project the QR
items.description: Display the QR slide on a screen or projector. Verify it is visible and scannable from a realistic distance.

items.title: Scan and Check
items.description: Scan with a phone, check the capture page loads, submit the form, and verify the contact and tag appear.

items.title: Receive Resource
items.description: Confirm the resource email arrives with working download link. Check formatting and personalization.

items.title: Test Booking
items.description: Open the booking link, choose a time, and confirm the calendar works. Cancel the test appointment afterward.

items.title: Check Exits
items.description: Verify workflow exit rules and unsubscribe function correctly. Test reply handling if configured.

items.title: Audience Size
items.description: Estimated number of attendees. This is your baseline for all other metrics.

items.title: QR Scans
items.description: How many times the QR was scanned. Note: scans indicate interest, not automatically individual leads.

items.title: Form Submissions
items.description: How many people completed the form. This is your actual lead count.

items.title: Emails Delivered
items.description: How many resource emails were successfully delivered.

items.title: Appointments Booked
items.description: How many people chose a time on your calendar.

items.title: Clients Gained
items.description: How many appointments converted to paying clients.

items.title: Sample Numbers
items.description: 100 attendees, 30 scans, 20 form submissions, 4 appointments, 1 new client.

items.title: Key Rate
items.description: Submissions to appointments: 4 ÷ 20 = 20%. This shows how well your nurture sequence converts interest to conversation.

items.title: Not Guaranteed
items.description: These are example numbers, not promised results. Your results will vary based on audience, talk quality, and offer relevance.

keyPoint: A system that has not been tested is a system that will fail. Project the QR, scan it, submit the form, receive the email, book a test appointment, and check every exit path. Then track real numbers: audience, scans, submissions, bookings, and clients. Data tells you what to improve; guessing wastes effort.

actionSteps.title: Complete the Dry Run
actionSteps.description: Walk through every step from QR scan to booking. Fix any issues before the real event.

actionSteps.title: Set Up Tracking

quizzes.question: What is the first step in the dry run?

options.option_text: Project the QR slide and verify it is scannable from a realistic distance
Send test emails to your entire contact list
Publish the funnel to social media
Book a real appointment with a colleague

quizzes.explanation: Start by projecting the QR slide and verifying it is visible and scannable. If the QR does not work in real venue conditions, the rest of the system is irrelevant.

quizzes.question: Which metric shows how well your nurture sequence converts interest to conversation?

options.option_text: Emails delivered divided by QR scans
QR scans divided by audience size
Clients gained divided by audience size
Appointments booked divided by form submissions

quizzes.explanation: Appointments booked ÷ form submissions shows your conversion from lead to conversation. This reveals how well your nurture sequence and offer resonate with interested people.

quizzes.question: Do QR scans automatically equal individual leads?

options.option_text: Yes, every scan creates a new lead record
No, scans indicate interest but do not create leads until the form is submitted
Only if the scanner has an account
Yes, but only on iPhones

quizzes.explanation: QR scans indicate interest but do not automatically create leads. The same person may scan multiple times. Only form submissions create contact records and trigger workflows.
